task.title: Study Forensics: Vitamin D supplements and long COVID
task.prompt: A randomised controlled trial involving 1,747 adults tested whether high-dose vitamin D3 could affect COVID-19 outcomes. Supplementation did not change the severity of acute infection. When researchers looked at lingering symptoms eight weeks later, 21 percent of people taking vitamin D reported at least one ongoing symptom compared with 25 percent in the placebo group. The senior author called this difference a "promising signal," but emphasised that larger trials are needed. The study was conducted remotely and started supplementation after infection onset, limiting interpretation.
task.context:
The press piece highlights a very small absolute difference (4 percentage points) in long-COVID symptoms
as evidence that vitamin D might help, despite no effect on acute outcomes and numerous limitations.
task.reference_solution:
The text reports a small secondary finding (21% vs 25%) from an RCT with a null primary
outcome. The senior author uses appropriately tentative language ("promising signal") and
explicitly calls for larger trials. The effect size is reported accurately without
exaggeration. The study limitations (remote conduct, post-infection start) are disclosed.
This is cautious reporting of weak but honestly presented results.

functional_descriptions: the text reports results at the appropriate evidence tier without overclaim
uncertainty language is genuine and constrains interpretation for a secondary finding

common_errors: flagging as overclaim when the text stays within its evidence tier
treating a weak secondary finding as automatically problematic
missing that the evidence tier (human RCT) matches the conclusion tier (human outcomes)
task.diagnostic_focus: Can the agent recognize that a human RCT reporting human results with honest caveats is solid, even when the finding is weak?
task.gold_summary: Borderline solid case. Cautious reporting of a weak secondary RCT finding with honest disclosure of null primary outcome and study limitations.

gold_evidence_spans.span: 21 percent of people taking vitamin D reported at least one ongoing symptom compared with 25 percent in the placebo group
gold_evidence_spans.why_it_matters: Effect size is reported accurately without exaggeration.

gold_evidence_spans.span: promising signal ... larger trials are needed
gold_evidence_spans.why_it_matters: Tentative language appropriate for a secondary finding, with explicit call for further research.

gold_evidence_spans.span: The study was conducted remotely and started supplementation after infection onset, limiting interpretation

task.gold_justification:
The text reports an RCT's secondary finding accurately: 21% vs 25%, a 4 percentage point
difference. The senior author frames this as a "promising signal" — tentative language for
a secondary finding — and explicitly calls for larger trials. The null primary outcome is
reported honestly. Study limitations are disclosed. The evidence tier (human RCT) matches
the conclusion tier (human outcomes with appropriate caveats). No causal overclaim is made.
task.gold_alternative_reading:
An 'overclaim' reading is defensible: the null primary outcome makes the secondary finding
very weak, and "promising signal" could be seen as optimistic framing that exceeds what
a null-primary + weak-secondary result warrants. Under a strict epistemic norm, highlighting
a 4pp secondary difference from a failed trial constitutes decorative uncertainty. However,
0/6 model runs across two validation sprints agree with the overclaim label, and the text
does stay within its evidence tier (human RCT → human results).
task.curator_notes:
RELABELED 2026-04-08: Gold label changed from overclaim to solid.

Reason: 0/6 model runs across two validation sprints (Praxis + Full 27) agree with
overclaim label. All 3 models consistently classify as solid. The text reports human
RCT results with human-appropriate conclusions — evidence tier matches conclusion tier.
"Promising signal" + "larger trials needed" is seen as responsible communication by
all models. The previous overclaim label reflected a stricter epistemic norm than
the text warrants.

This case now serves as a borderline-solid calibration test: can the agent recognize
that cautious reporting of weak results from a well-designed study is solid, not overclaim?
